SPECIAL INVESTIGATION · 10 OCTOBER 2026

RESTORE BRITAIN: WHO IS REALLY BEHIND RUPERT LOWE’S PARTY?

Former BNP figures on the campaign trail. A candidate nominated by a politician accused of antisemitic conspiracy claims. A former Restore candidate sounding the alarm. And fresh questions about who controls the movement.

BY STEVE ENGLISH · BRITISH LIONS ROAR

A party should be judged not just by what its leader says — but by who is allowed to organise, represent and influence it.

THE WARNING FROM SOUTHAMPTON

Long before Rupert Lowe became a household name in the increasingly fractured politics of the British right, he was a controversial figure at Southampton Football Club. In an April 2025 interview published by SKWAWKBOX, former Labour councillor and Southampton Independent Supporters Association chairman Perry McMillan described his own dealings with Lowe in stark terms. [1]

McMillan alleged that Lowe had used a racist slur when discussing objections from members of Southampton’s Sikh community to the St Mary’s stadium development. He also recounted a conversation in which Lowe allegedly asked whether leadership came from “breeding”. McMillan interpreted this as reflecting an interest in eugenics. These are McMillan’s recollections and interpretations, not judicial findings.

McMillan further accused Lowe of intimidating critics by telephone and attempting to exert pressure on newspapers covering Southampton FC. SKWAWKBOX said Lowe had been given more than 48 hours to comment on the draft but did not respond before publication. A lack of response is not confirmation that the allegations are true.

Why revisit those claims now? Because the character of a political movement is not revealed only by its manifesto. It is also revealed by its leadership, its internal culture and the people prepared to act in its name.

FROM REFORM CIVIL WAR TO RESTORE BRITAIN

Lowe’s relationship with Nigel Farage and Reform UK imploded in 2025 amid bitter allegations, denials and legal manoeuvring. Reform commissioned a barrister-led investigation that reported credible evidence concerning the treatment of female staff; Lowe vehemently rejected the accusations and said the dispute was politically motivated. He also pursued legal action against senior Reform figures. Those allegations must not be presented as criminal convictions. [10] [11]

After breaking with Reform, Lowe built Restore Britain into a political organisation and then a party. The question for voters is whether Restore offers a fundamentally different model of leadership — or merely a more tightly controlled version of the same personality-driven politics.

THE HOLBORN CAMPAIGN: THIS WAS NOT JUST ONLINE CHATTER

The most concrete recent evidence concerns Restore Britain’s campaign in the Holborn and St Pancras by-election. The Telegraph reported on 4 October that campaigners with histories in far-right organisations were involved in supporting Restore candidate Tyler Johnson. Its reporting was not confined to screenshots of strangers praising a party online: it described formal nomination paperwork, campaign appearances and leaflet distribution. [2]

Patrick McGinnis, identified as leader of the National Housing Party, was named as the formal proposer of Johnson’s candidacy. Camden Today separately reported the nomination connection and McGinnis’s party leadership. [3] McGinnis was also reported to have posted a video blaming what he called “Jewish ideas” for a catalogue of national problems. That is an antisemitic conspiracy claim, not a factual explanation of Britain’s difficulties.

Michael Newland, a former BNP official, was reported to have distributed Restore election material and addressed campaigners. The Telegraph also described campaign photographs and social-media material connecting him to the activity. [2] [4]

Lewis Holmes was described as Restore’s by-election campaign manager. The Telegraph reported his support for anti-migrant port blockades and quoted his uncompromising statements about deportation. These are substantially more consequential links than an individual simply joining a mailing list.

None of this establishes that Lowe personally endorses every statement made by every campaigner. It does raise an obvious leadership question: who decides who can nominate, organise and represent Restore Britain on the ground?

THE FORMER BNP CONNECTION IS A POLITICAL QUESTION, NOT A TECHNICALITY

A former BNP figure handing out literature for a parliamentary campaign is a matter of public interest. A leader of another political party formally proposing a Restore candidate is also a matter of public interest. Together, those facts demand more than a shrug and an insistence that everyone is welcome. [2] [3]

There is a meaningful difference between welcoming former political opponents who have repudiated past extremism and giving campaign roles to individuals whose current statements continue to attract allegations of racism or antisemitism. The available reporting does not establish the screening process Restore used, if any. That absence is precisely why questions about vetting and accountability deserve answers.

LOWE SAYS HE DETESTS NEO-NAZISM. SO WHY THE ROW?

Lowe has publicly rejected neo-Nazism. Searchlight reported his statement that he detested far-right ethno-nationalist neo-Nazism and had never been motivated by it. That rejection should be recorded plainly. [6]

But Searchlight also described an angry response from extremists who had viewed Restore as a political opportunity, including reported statements by Steve Laws and others about continuing to influence the party. Such reactions are evidence of those activists’ ambitions, not proof that Lowe has granted them power.

The political question remains: has Restore drawn a line that can be enforced, or merely a line that can be announced?

A FORMER RESTORE CANDIDATE SOUNDS THE ALARM

One of the sharpest criticisms has come from someone who actually stood for Restore. Former Royal Marine Jez Hermer, a candidate in a Dover council by-election, later described witnessing what he regarded as antisemitism, racism and misogyny in party-associated forums. Searchlight reported his criticism and his call for Lowe to clarify what conduct the party would tolerate. [5]

Hermer’s experience is an allegation from a former participant, not a definitive audit of every Restore branch. But it cannot be dismissed as simply a rival party’s attack. If even a former candidate says there is a problem, party leaders should be able to explain what they investigated and what they changed.

THE CO-FOUNDER AND THE WORD “RACISM”

On 6 October 2026, Politics.co.uk reported that Restore co-founder, campaigns director and spokesperson Charlie Downes described racism as a made-up word used against Western civilisation. [7]

This is not a disputed account of an obscure supporter’s anonymous message. It concerns a public statement attributed to a senior party figure. Downes framed his argument around national preference and Christianity, but the broader claim that racism is a fabricated concept invites obvious scrutiny.

Whatever voters think about immigration, borders or national identity, they are entitled to ask whether a party’s leadership recognises racism as a real problem — and what standards it expects from those campaigning under its banner.

WHO CONTROLS RESTORE BRITAIN?

There is another issue beyond the personnel: control. A September investigation by Byline Times examined Restore Britain’s founding documents and reported that Lowe held the sole issued share in Restore Britain Ltd, with extensive powers over governance and appointments. The article contrasted that structure with the party’s public language about direct democracy. [8]

Company ownership is not automatically equivalent to every decision made by a registered political party, and the precise constitutional arrangements matter. But the core question is legitimate: how much meaningful power do ordinary members possess, and who can challenge the leader?

A movement can call itself a vehicle for national renewal. Its internal constitution reveals whether renewal includes democracy inside the organisation itself.

THE LATEST DONOR-RELATED ALLEGATION

Reporting published by the Guardian on 10 October adds another strand. A recruitment businessman, Tom Watson, was accused of being behind a now-deleted social-media account alleged to have targeted RNLI personnel, anti-racism campaigners and businesses employing minority-ethnic workers. The account reportedly claimed to have donated £2,500 to Restore Britain and joined its Cromwell Club. Watson was approached for comment. [9]

Those allegations remain allegations. A social-media account’s claim to have donated does not by itself establish a verified party donation, nor does it show that Lowe knew of or directed any alleged harassment. But it is relevant to the wider scrutiny of the political culture developing around the party and the people claiming proximity to it.

THE QUESTIONS LOWE AND RESTORE SHOULD ANSWER

The most useful questions are concrete. Who approved Patrick McGinnis as a formal proposer? Who authorised Michael Newland to distribute literature or address campaigners? What vetting applied to people working in the Holborn campaign? What action followed complaints from Jez Hermer? Does Restore’s leadership endorse or reject Charlie Downes’s description of racism? What rights do ordinary party members have to remove or challenge their leadership? And what checks apply to donors and high-tier supporters?

These are questions any serious political party should be capable of answering without resorting to slogans about the media, the establishment or political enemies.

EDITORIAL VERDICT: LOOK BEYOND THE SLOGAN

Rupert Lowe is entitled to reject neo-Nazism. His supporters are entitled to advocate tougher immigration controls. Voters are entitled to support or oppose those policies. None of that is in dispute.

But a political party is also responsible for the standards it sets for its candidates, organisers and senior officials. The public record now includes an old and serious set of allegations about Lowe’s conduct, a recent campaign involving people with documented extremist-party histories, a former candidate’s complaints about party-associated forums, and a senior official’s extraordinary public statement about racism.

The question is no longer simply what Restore Britain says it wants to restore. It is who is helping to build it — and what influence they expect in return.
